title: A Detroit techno record
description: One track built from nothing, a lesson at a time: pulse, strings, the chord, rolling hats, bass, variation, sections, the mix.
author: Strudel Workshop

tracks.title: A Detroit techno record
tracks.blurb: Every lesson starts from the code you finished in the one before, and the last one is a whole record.

lessons.title: The pulse
lessons.goal: Start the record: a 909 kick and quiet open hats at 128 BPM.
lessons.concept:
Detroit techno was made by three high-school friends from Belleville, Michigan: **Juan Atkins**, **Derrick May** and **Kevin Saunderson**. They heard Kraftwerk and Parliament on the same radio show and built a music that was both: machine-steady and soulful.

It begins where every techno record begins, with the **pulse**: a TR-909 kick on every beat and open hats on the offbeats. We set `const key` now so every pitched part later agrees. This whole track grows across the next seven lessons; each one starts from the code you finish here.

tasks.text: Add a part called kick: a TR-909 kick on every beat.
Add a part called hats: open hats on the offbeats, quiet.
tasks.hint: const hats = s("[~ oh]*4").bank("RolandTR909").gain(.4), and stack(kick, hats).

summary: Techno starts with a steady 909 pulse.
const key up front keeps every later part in tune.

lessons.title: The strings
lessons.goal: Add the Detroit string pad: wide, slow and high-passed.
lessons.concept:
The sound that made Detroit different from Chicago was **strings**: synthesized string pads borrowed from Italo disco and film scores, floating over the drums. Derrick May’s *Strings of Life* is named for them.

A **supersaw** chord with a slow **attack** and a long **release** does the job. Strings carry no low end, so a **high-pass filter** at 300 Hz takes the mud out and leaves room for the kick. Scale degrees `0,2,4,6` in the key give a minor seventh chord.

tasks.text: Add a part called strings: a four-note chord in the key on a supersaw, soft, with a slow attack and a long release.

summary: Detroit strings: a supersaw chord with slow attack and release.
High-pass pads so they never fight the kick.

lessons.title: The chord
lessons.goal: Add a short minor-ninth stab on the offbeats of 2 and 4.
lessons.concept:
Under the strings sits the **stab**: a chord hit short and hard. Detroit favoured the **minor ninth**, five notes that sound both dark and bright. Kevin Saunderson’s Inner City records are full of them.

Scale degrees `0,2,4,6,8` build it in the key. A **square** wave gives a hollow, synthetic tone; a quick **decay** with no **sustain** makes it a stab rather than a pad; a low-pass filter rounds its top off.

tasks.text: Add a part called stab: a five-note chord in the key on a square wave, on the offbeats of beats 2 and 4.
tasks.hint: const stab = n("[0,2,4,6,8]").scale(key).s("square").struct("[~ x]*2").gain(.4), and stack it.

tasks.text: Make it a stab: quick decay, no sustain.
Round it off with a low-pass at 1200 Hz.

summary: The Detroit stab is a minor ninth, hit short.
Short decay and no sustain turn a chord into a stab.

lessons.title: Rolling hats
lessons.goal: Add 16th hats with accents and a light swing.
lessons.concept:
What makes a techno groove **roll** is the hi-hat line: closed hats on every 16th, louder on the beat, with a touch of **swing** so the grid breathes. The 909’s hats were sampled from real cymbals, which is why they cut through.

A **gain pattern** in quotes sets a level per step; `.swingBy(.14, 8)` pushes every second 16th a little late, about 57% on an MPC.

tasks.text: Add a part called ticks: closed hats on every 16th with a gain pattern that accents the beat.
tasks.hint: const ticks = s("hh*16").bank("RolandTR909").gain("[.5 .25 .35 .25]*4"), and stack it.

summary: 16th hats with accents make a techno groove roll.

lessons.title: The bass in the gaps
lessons.goal: Add an offbeat bass in the key, short and filtered.
lessons.concept:
Detroit bass lines sit **between the kicks**, on the offbeats, so the low end never doubles up. The notes come from the same key as the strings and the stab, which is what `const key` was for.

A **sawtooth** two octaves down, with a short envelope and a low-pass around 600 Hz, is round and heavy. The pattern `[~ 0] [~ 0] [~ 3] [~ 5]` walks the root, the fourth and the fifth of the scale.

tasks.text: Add a part called bass: scale degrees in the key on a sawtooth, two octaves down, on every offbeat.
tasks.hint: const bass = n("[~ 0] [~ 0] [~ 3] [~ 5]").scale(key).s("sawtooth").octave(2), and stack it.

tasks.text: Make it short and dark: quick decay, no sustain, low-pass at 600 Hz.

summary: Offbeat bass keeps the low end clear of the kick.
Scale degrees in the shared key keep bass and chords agreeing.

lessons.title: Variation every eight
lessons.goal: Add a two-bar clap and a hat fill every eighth bar.
lessons.concept:
A loop that never changes is a demo, not a record. Detroit tracks change on the **phrase**: every two bars a small difference, every eight a **fill**.

`<a b>` alternates two patterns bar by bar, so the clap can answer itself. `.lastOf(8, x => x.ply(2))` doubles every hat in the last bar of every eight: a roll that announces the next phrase.

tasks.text: Add a part called clap: a 909 clap on 2 and 4 in odd bars, with an extra double hit in even bars.
tasks.hint: const clap = s("<[~ cp ~ cp] [~ cp ~ [cp cp]]>").bank("RolandTR909").gain(.6), and stack it.

tasks.text: Make the hats roll in the last bar of every eight.
tasks.hint: .lastOf(8, x => x.ply(2)) on the ticks line.

summary: .lastOf(8, f) changes the last bar of every eight.

lessons.title: Sections
lessons.goal: Name the sections and arrange them, with a breakdown that drops the kick.
lessons.concept:
Detroit records are built for DJs and dancers alike: a drums-only **intro** to mix into, a long **main** section, a **breakdown** where the kick leaves and the strings take over, and an **outro** to mix out of.

A section is a named `stack`. `arrange([16, intro], …)` plays each one for that many bars; every section restarts its own clock.

tasks.text: Name four sections: intro (kick, hats, ticks), main (everything), breakdown (strings, stab, clap: no kick) and outro (kick, hats). Keep playing main for now.
tasks.hint: const intro = stack(kick, hats, ticks), const main = stack(kick, hats, ticks, strings, stab, bass, clap), const breakdown = stack(strings, stab, clap), const outro = stack(kick, hats); end the code with main.

tasks.text: Arrange them: 16 bars of intro, 32 of main, 16 of breakdown, 16 of outro.
tasks.hint: Replace the last line with arrange([16, intro], [32, main], [16, breakdown], [16, outro]).

summary: Sections are named stacks; arrange() plays them in turn.
A breakdown drops the kick and lets the strings carry the room.

lessons.title: Project: The mix
lessons.goal: Clear the low end, set the levels and finish the arrangement.
lessons.concept:
Mixing in Strudel means three things: **cut what a part doesn’t need** (high-pass the hats), **keep every level under the kick** (nothing above .8 but the kick itself), and give the record its full **shape**.

A fifth section, a **build** where the strings join the drums before the main section, makes the first drop land. Five sections, 96 bars: a record you could play out.

tasks.text: High-pass both hat parts at 400 Hz.
tasks.hint: .hpf(400) on the hats line and on the ticks line.

tasks.text: Set the bass level to .7, so nothing but the kick is above .8.
Add a build section (kick, hats, ticks, strings) between the intro and main, and arrange all five: 16, 16, 32, 16, 16.
tasks.hint: const build = stack(kick, hats, ticks, strings), then arrange([16, intro], [16, build], [32, main], [16, breakdown], [16, outro]).

summary: High-pass what has no low end; keep every level under the kick.
A build before the main section makes the drop land.
